title: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
text:
One day Rabbi Yochanan was bathing in the Jordan when Resh Lakish, then a bandit and gladiator of enormous strength, leapt into the river after him. Yochanan said, "Your strength should be for Torah." Resh Lakish answered, "Your beauty should be for women." Yochanan offered him his sister, more beautiful than himself, if he would change his life. Resh Lakish agreed. Yochanan taught him, and he became one of the greatest scholars of his generation, Yochanan's study partner and brother-in-law.

Years later, in the study hall, they disagreed about when weapons such as swords and knives become finished objects in law. Yochanan said one thing, Resh Lakish another. Then Yochanan snapped, "A bandit knows his trade." Resh Lakish was deeply hurt by the reminder of his past. Yochanan was hurt in turn, Resh Lakish fell ill, and Yochanan refused even his sister's pleas to pray for him. Resh Lakish died.

Yochanan sank into grief. The sages sent him a brilliant scholar, Elazar ben Pedat, who supported every statement Yochanan made with a source. "Are you like the son of Lakish?" Yochanan cried. "When I said something, he raised twenty-four objections, I gave twenty-four answers, and the law became clear." He went about tearing his clothes and weeping, "Where are you, son of Lakish?" until he lost his mind, and the sages prayed for his death.
lesson: In a close friendship, one contemptuous remark about the other's past can cut deeper than any argument. Value the friend who challenges you, and repair hurts while you still can.
